<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README you provided, Tracee is an open source runtime security tool built on eBPF that monitors and analyzes system events for security and observability. Its purpose is to “tap” into the Linux kernel using eBPF probes, collect a wealth of system and security events, process them (including rule-based and signature-based detections), and then present or export that information via various interfaces (CLI, gRPC, HTTP) or integrations (e.g., Docker, Kubernetes, Prometheus, Grafana).

Below is how to build a system design diagram that illustrates the architecture clearly:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Kernel eBPF Layer: Represent the eBPF probes that live in the kernel and collect the raw system events. This includes the C files in pkg/ebpf (such as tracee.bpf.c) and supporting header files.
   • Loader/Initialization Module: Show the user-space component (in pkg/cmd/initialize and cmd/tracee-ebpf) that loads the eBPF programs into the kernel and sets up callbacks.
   • Event Collection & Processing Engine: Depict the core modules (in pkg/events, pkg/bufferdecoder, pkg/ebpf/events_pipeline, and pkg/filters) that capture, decode, and enrich the raw events.
   • Signature/Rule Engine: Outline the modules in pkg/signatures and pkg/policy (including the tracee-rules command in cmd/tracee-rules) that analyze events against pre-defined security signatures and rules.
   • API Layer & External Interfaces: Include the gRPC server (pkg/server/grpc) and the HTTP server (pkg/server/http) as methods to expose processed events and telemetry information. Also note the CLI entrypoints (cmd/tracee variants) for direct tool interaction.
   • Container & Kubernetes Integration: Acknowledge the modules under pkg/containers as well as the Kubernetes CRD and helm charts under deploy/helm and deploy/kubernetes. Also include integration points for container runtimes (docker, containerd, crio).
   • Observability & Metrics: Indicate support for metrics collection (pkg/metrics) as well as the Prometheus/Grafana dashboard configurations (performance/dashboard) for performance and monitoring.
   • Auxiliary Libraries: Recognize supporting modules such as logging (pkg/logger), error formatting (pkg/errfmt), and utility functions (pkg/utils).

2. Determine Relationships and Data Flow:
   • Draw directional arrows from the Kernel eBPF layer to the Loader/Initialization module, showing how the tool inserts its probes.
   • Illustrate the flow of raw event data from the eBPF layer to the Event Processing Engine.
   • From the event processing block, send the data to both the Signature/Rule Engine (for security analysis) and to the Output/API modules.
   • Show separate flows from the API/CLI components to external consumers (e.g., CLI dashboard, gRPC clients, HTTP clients).
   • Represent additional integration arrows to external systems and dashboards (e.g., Prometheus, Grafana, Kubernetes deployments).

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular Design: Emphasize the clear separation between the kernel-level (eBPF probes) and the user-level processing components.
   • Loose Coupling: Note the independent modules in the policy/signature engine, event processing, CLI/API, and container integration.
   • Extensibility: Identify the “rules” and “signatures” components (tracee-rules and pkg/signatures) that are designed to be extended with minimal impact on the core pipeline.
   • Integration with External Tools: Show how the tool is packaged (via Docker, Helm charts), thus reinforcing the “cloud-native” design for container and Kubernetes environments.

4. Include Relevant Technologies, Frameworks, or Libraries:
   • Go (Golang) as the main programming language.
   • eBPF via Linux for kernel-level event collection.
   • gRPC and HTTP for API servers.
   • Helm charts and Kubernetes manifests for deployment.
   • Docker for containerized execution.
   • Prometheus and Grafana for observability and performance dashboards.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram to This Specific Project:
   • For this open-source observability and security tool:
       – Emphasize the split between the kernel (eBPF probes) and the multiple user-level pipelines (event processing, signature checking, rule evaluation, etc.).
       – Show how these pieces interact synchronously (for real-time event monitoring) and asynchronously (for metrics collection or dashboard updates).
       – Depict deployment components like Docker, Helm, and Kubernetes separately to indicate how Tracee is packaged and deployed.
   • Use different colored boxes or distinct shapes to differentiate:
       – Kernel-level components (e.g., use a darker color or hexagon shapes).
       – User-space processing modules.
       – API/external interface components.
       – Integration/deployment components.

6. Instructions for the Principal Software Engineer:
   • Begin by sketching out a high-level “box diagram” that contains the key layers:
         • Kernel eBPF Probes → Event Loader/Collector → Processing & Enrichment Engine → Signature/Rule Engine → Output & API Layers.
   • Place additional elements for container integration and observability (metrics, dashboards) connected to the API/Output node.
   • Clearly label each box with the corresponding package or module names (for example, “pkg/ebpf”, “pkg/events”, “pkg/signatures”, “pkg/server”).
   • Draw directional arrows to indicate the flow of information/data. For instance, from “Kernel eBPF Probes” to “Event Processing Engine”, then splitting into multiple outputs like CLI, gRPC, and HTTP.
   • Consider color coding or different shapes (e.g., circles for integration points, rectangles for processing modules) to visually demarcate different types of components.
   • Include notes on any external services (e.g., “Kubernetes API”, “Prometheus”, “Grafana”) and how they integrate by consuming the events and metrics.
   • Finally, detail the interactions between the various developer tools (e.g., Makefiles, Dockerfiles) as part of the deployment and CI/CD pipeline, if relevant, on a separate sub-diagram or annotation area.

By following these guidelines and ensuring every major component is represented with clear relationships and labels, you will produce an accurate, detailed system design diagram that captures the essential architecture of Tracee.
</explanation>
